messages:
incident-bot: Pager: HIGH — generation-service p99 latency > SLO (3s) across us-west-2. Auto-escalate to oncall.

alice (oncall): I'm awake, looking now. Seeing p95 jump and streaming stalls reported by clients. Starting triage — marking impacted customers in thread.

sam (prod-support): Customer 'TextFlow' reported repeated websocket disconnects and partial outputs. They saw streaming stalls around 10:05 PDT.

ben (sre): Graphs: p95 from ~120ms -> 700ms, p99 from ~450ms -> 3.2s. Spike started at ~10:02 and correlated with CPU on gpu-serve-*-pods and high KV cache miss/eviction rates.

carla (ml-runtime): Noted large increase in KV cache evictions and fragment count on runtime nodes. Prefill rates are low vs decode allocation — looks like prefill workers didn't keep up. Suspect fragmentation/eviction churn.

linda (eng): Any recent rollouts? I deployed an optimize patch last night to change the KV eviction algorithm to LRU-approximator. Could that interact badly with bursts?

ben (sre): Checking deploy history... linda's change rolled at 02:11 UTC (yesterday). Rollout traffic % 100. Coincidence but could be related.

alice (oncall): Repro steps: tail logs on a hot node:
```
[2025-11-03T10:03:05Z] KVCache: entries=1_180_342 fragments=83_220 evictions/sec=5_120
[2025-11-03T10:03:05Z] PrefillWorker: queue_len=12 decode_worker_busy=98%
[2025-11-03T10:03:06Z] Serve: stream_stall client=ws://... conn=1245 duration=1.2s
```

carla (ml-runtime): That fragments number is huge — fragmentation implies many small allocations. Looks like prefill is producing many tiny cache entries instead of consolidated prefixes. Could be a hash collision or key-normalization bug from the change.

sam (prod-support): Impact: 3 mid-market customers saw degraded quality/latency for ~10-20% of requests. No data leak, just latency and partial streams. Notifying PMs.

alice (oncall): Immediate mitigations: 1) Roll back linda's eviction patch on a small canary set? 2) Increase KV cache capacity for hot pool 3) Throttle streaming to fallback synchronous path for critical customers. Opinions?

ben (sre): I'd avoid full rollback without canary. We can patch config to increase `kv_cache_max_entries` and reduce `kv_fragmentation_threshold` to force coalescing. Also increase prefill worker replicas temporarily.

linda (eng): Pushing a config patch now to canary (us-west-2a) to set `kv_cache_max_entries=2e6` and `prefill_replicas=4` and `prefill_batch_ms=10` to speed prefill.

devops-bot: Deploy started: linda/kv-prefill-tune -> canary us-west-2a. CI passed. Rolling update: 2->4 pods.

alice (oncall): After canary rollout, metrics in 2 minutes?

ben (sre): Canary shows lower eviction/sec (5_120 -> 430) and fragments down by ~60%. p95 improved to ~200ms, p99 to ~700ms in that AZ.

carla (ml-runtime): Good sign. But still seeing decode latency spikes for some long-context requests. There is prefill vs decode imbalance: decoders are still saturating because batching algorithm favors decode over prefill under high concurrency.

alice (oncall): Next step: propagate config change to other AZs and bump prefill capacity cluster-wide. Also enable fallback for top-tier customers: route them to dedicated nodes with pinned cache.

sam (prod-support): I've enabled customer routing to dedicated pool for TextFlow and two other customers. They confirm streaming is back to normal for their sessions.

ben (sre): I'll schedule a controlled rollback of the eviction algorithm (linda's patch) for a full rollback window if the config changes don't hold. For now, config change + scale seems to mitigate.

linda (eng): Opening PR to revert eviction patch and add stronger unit tests for key normalization. Also adding telemetry: `kv_key_size_histogram` and `kv_fragment_coalesced` counters.

carla (ml-runtime): Post-mortem notes: root cause likely combinatorial — small change to eviction heuristics exposed prefill batching inefficiencies and a key-normalization edge causing many tiny cache entries. Result: fragmentation -> eviction churn -> more cache misses -> more decode work -> streaming stalls -> tail latency.

alice (oncall): Action items (assigned):
- ben: Monitor p95/p99 and eviction rates for 24h and run alert if p99 > 1.5s (assigned)
- linda: PR to revert + tests + telemetry (assigned)
- carla: Tune batcher to prefer prefill under high kv miss scenarios and add canary test (assigned)
- sam: Customer outreach notes and incident summary draft (assigned)

ben (sre): I'll also add a temporary alert: `kv_eviction_rate > 1000/s AND p99 > 1s` to catch recurrence.

devops-bot: Canary rollout completed successfully across us-west-2a, propagating to other AZs per manual approval.

alice (oncall): Propagated to all AZs. p95 now ~160-220ms, p99 ~450-750ms cluster-wide. We'll keep monitoring.

sam (prod-support): Customers updated; PMs and Sales looped in. No immediate refunds requested.

linda (eng): Post-fix notes: I found an edge-case in key normalization where trailing null bytes produced distinct keys for the same prefix. Fix included in revert PR.

carla (ml-runtime): Recommend long-term: 1) stronger prefill autoscaling 2) prefer prefill over decode when eviction churn detected 3) add background KV coalescer to compact small fragments 4) add chaos tests that simulate fragmentation.

alice (oncall): Great. Closing the pager for now — we have mitigations and owners. Will convert thread to incident channel and start a formal postmortem doc.

ben (sre): Adding timeline and raw metrics to the postmortem doc. Will include config diffs and git SHAs.

incident-bot: Incident resolved — status: mitigated, severity: high -> monitoring. Duration: ~46 minutes. Link to incident doc: <https://redwood.internal/incidents/INC-2025-11-03-kv-frag>

alice (oncall): Thanks everyone. I'll hand off to oncall rotation for overnight monitoring. @linda @carla please coordinate on the revert PR.

linda (eng): On it. Going to draft the revert and tests now.

carla (ml-runtime): I'll add the canary test infra overnight.

sam (prod-support): Filing customer follow-ups and notes in CRM.

alice (oncall): End of thread.
